title: Plant responses to stay in balance

draft.title: Plant responses to stay in balance
card: Plants lose water as vapour, mostly through stomata. Stomata are small pores in the leaf surface, each opened and closed by a pair of guard cells.
When a plant is short of water, its guard cells lose water and become less swollen. The stomata close, so less water vapour escapes.
In a longer drought, some plants drop leaves. Fewer leaves means less surface area for water loss.
These responses keep the plant's water level steady. Closed stomata also reduce the carbon dioxide entering the leaf, so there is a trade-off with photosynthesis.
draft.remember: A plant short of water loses less of it by closing stomata and, in drought, by dropping leaves.

a.q: Why does closing its stomata help a plant in a dry spell?
opts: Less water vapour escapes from the leaves
More water is drawn up from the soil by the roots
The guard cells swell and store extra water
More carbon dioxide can enter the leaf
a.why: Stomata are the main exit for water vapour, so closing them cuts water loss. Carbon dioxide entry does not increase: closed stomata reduce it, which is the cost to photosynthesis.
a.clue: Think about where water vapour leaves the leaf.

b.q: A eucalypt in a long drought in western NSW drops many of its leaves. How does this help the tree stay in water balance?
opts: It reduces the leaf surface area that loses water
It lets the stomata stay open to take in more carbon dioxide
It makes the guard cells swell so stomata close
It lets the tree make more food by photosynthesis
b.why: Fewer leaves means less surface for water to escape, so the tree loses less water over the drought. Dropping leaves does not help photosynthesis: with fewer leaves, the tree has less area to make food.
b.clue: Fewer leaves means less of what?

a.best: Less water vapour escapes from the leaves

b.best: It reduces the leaf surface area that loses water
